readerTitle: Why pricing at the average guess earns less
caseNote: 가상 사례 (브런치 카페, 구독형 앱) + 실제 연구 경향 (가상 응답 편향) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 지불 의향은 하나의 숫자가 아니라 고객마다 다른 값의 분포이고, 가격은 그 분포 위에 긋는 선이다.
misconception: 고객들이 낼 수 있다고 답한 금액의 평균을 가격으로 정하면 가장 많이 번다.

sources.text: List, J. A. & Gallet, C. A. (2001). What Experimental Protocol Influence Disparities Between Actual and Hypothetical Stated Values? Environmental and Resource Economics.
카페와 앱의 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 가상 응답 편향(설문에서 말한 금액이 실제 지불보다 높게 나오는 경향)은 List & Gallet(2001) 메타분석 등에서 보고됩니다. 편향의 크기는 연구마다 다르므로 카드에는 구체적 배수를 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 서지 정보를 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: Why pricing at the average guess earns less
body: A café owner asks 100 brunch regulars what they'd pay for a new weekend set menu. The answers average $21.
So she prices it at $21. It's a sensible move, and it leaves money on the table. The average hides the number that matters.

image.label: Brunch plate with many different price tags floating above it
image.brief: 브런치 접시 하나 위로 $12, $18, $24, $30 가격표가 여러 개 떠 있고, 각 가격표 옆에 서로 다른 손님 얼굴 실루엣. 따뜻한 카페 톤. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: Which price earns the most?
body: Of the 100 regulars, 15 would pay up to $30, 40 up to $24, 25 up to $18, and 20 up to $12. Each plate costs $8 in food and prep.
Which price leaves the most money after food costs?

options.feedback: It feels fair to everyone, but only 55 people will pay it, and you earn just $13 on each of them. Total: $715.
Same 55 buyers as at $21, but $3 more per plate. Total: $880. You lose nobody extra by going higher.
You serve 80 people and earn $800. More full tables, but less money and more work than $24.

cards.title: Money left after food costs, by price
body: Between $18 and $24, nobody drops out. Moving the price up to $24 is pure gain.

cards.title: Willingness to pay
body: **Willingness to pay** is the most a customer would pay for something before walking away. Every customer has their own number.
Line those numbers up from highest to lowest and you get demand. A price is just a line you draw across it: everyone above says yes, everyone below says no.

image.label: Staircase of customers sorted by what they'd pay, with a price line across
image.brief: 손님 100명을 지불 의향 순으로 계단처럼 세운 그림. $30, $24, $18, $12 네 계단. $24 높이에 가로선을 긋고, 선 위 손님은 초록, 아래 손님은 회색으로 표시.

cards.title: Gaps matter more than the average.
body: The average blends people who would never meet at the same price. Nobody in this group would pay exactly $21.

What earns money is where customers bunch up. Forty people sit at $24, so any price below that gives away dollars without winning anyone new. The best price usually sits just at the top of a big group, not in the middle of everyone.

cards.title: Watch what people pay, not what they say.
body: Asking "what would you pay?" is a weak guide. Research on **hypothetical bias** finds people often name higher amounts in surveys than they actually pay when real money is involved.
Better signals come from behavior: test two prices on different days, note who orders the premium option, and watch what happens after a price change.

image.label: Survey sheet versus a real receipt, side by side
image.brief: 왼쪽에 설문지("I'd pay $25!"), 오른쪽에 실제 영수증($18). 둘 사이에 차이를 보여주는 물음표 대신 저울 아이콘. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Willingness to pay moves, and cutting people out costs something.
body: Each person's number shifts with the situation: a nearby rival, a holiday, a bad week. Today's map can be wrong next month.
At $24, 45 regulars stop ordering the set menu. Some may leave entirely, empty tables look bad, and fewer guests means fewer coffees and pastries. Count those effects before you trust the chart.

cards.title: Now it's a budgeting app.
body: Your budgeting app has thousands of free users. In a survey, the average user said they'd pay $15 a month for a premium plan.
How do you set the price?

options.feedback: Quick and simple, but it trusts a stated average. Users usually pay less than they say, and the average hides where they actually bunch up.

options.text: Show new signups $9, $15 or $24 at random and compare how many pay
options.feedback: Real money reveals real willingness to pay and shows where users cluster. It takes a few weeks and some careful handling of fairness.

options.text: Run a longer, more detailed survey first
options.feedback: You learn more about what users value, but you still only learn what they say, not what they pay.

cards.title: A price is a line across many different numbers.
body: Every customer carries a different maximum. Find where they bunch up, and price at the top of a big group, not at the average.
**Try it today:** for one product, sort your customers into three or four groups by what you think each would pay. Where is the biggest group?
